newsitem.title: UK: Turkey mark bond succeeds, lira deal another story.
newsitem.headline: Turkey mark bond succeeds, lira deal another story.

text.p: Turkey successfully sold a 500 million mark bond on Wednesday despite the possibility of a rating cut by Moody's, dealers said.

But factors such as large amounts of expatriate Turkish funds in Germany and favourable tax treatment contributed to its success, and their absence may make deals in other currencies harder to sell, they said.
"Turkey did well in marks for very specific reasons," said a syndicate head at a European bank. "Its planned lira deal will be a more difficult trade due to the rating uncertainties."

Bankers at joint lead managers Commerzbank and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the seven-year mark bond had been well received and the price had traded up already. "It was a grand success," an official at Commerzbank in Frankfurt said. "About 80 percent of the deal was sold in Germany. Turkish bonds are popular with Turkish people here and other retail investors."
A double tax treaty between Turkey and Germany offered tax advantages for some buyers on interest earned, he said.

A banker at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said: "It was a complete blow-out. Demand was not affected by Turkey being on Moody's creditwatch. The last mark bond we did was 750 million marks, so we did back off a little bit on size this time."
On January 10 Moody's Investors Service said it was considering cutting Turkey's Ba3 long-term foreign currency debt rating. Turkey is rated B by Standard and Poor's Corp.

Moody's said its move was related to the continuing deterioration of Turkey's fiscal situation and the apparent inability of the authorities to take measures that would address the structural causes of the budget deficit.

Turkey responded by saying its ratings should be based on its 1997 plans and take into account deviations from targets following its 1994 financial crisis and the problems of trying to form a government in 1996.
Turkey plans to raise $2.0 billion in the international capital markets this year after borrowing $2.9 billion in 1996.
Its next scheduled deal is the lira offering, a 500 billion lire five-year bond due at the end of February or early March.
